response: ## Review: `src/assets/hero-banner.png` **Finding:** `crime_00011` — Oversized Raster (`oversized_raster`, universal pack), confidence 0.95, effort `quick`. **Size, quoted from the evidence:** > `byte size: 260,000 bytes (253.9 KB)` > `severity ladder: low ≥ 200 KB · medium ≥ 500 KB · high ≥ 1000 KB` > `format: png` ### Verdict: request changes — don't block 253.9 KB sits just over the low rung of the ladder (200 KB), a quarter of the way to `high`. That is not a merge-stopping asset on its own, and `crimes` correctly scores it `severity: low` / `effort: quick`. What raises it above "file a follow-up" is context the detector can't see: this is *the landing-page hero*. It's almost certainly the LCP element, so its bytes land on the critical path for every first-time visitor, uncached, often on mobile. A 254 KB PNG as LCP is a real Core Web Vitals cost, and the fix is a five-minute re-encode with zero code risk. So: **request changes, fix in this PR.** Blocking (`verdict`-style fail) would be disproportionate for a low-severity asset finding — reserve that for the `high` findings in this scan, e.g. `crime_00001` (`svg_with_embedded_raster` on `partner-logo.svg`, severity `high`), which is the same asset-pipeline problem wearing a vector costume. ### The transformation **One caveat first:** unlike `crime_00013` (which reports `dimensions: 32 × 32 px` for `check-icon.png`), this finding gives byte size and format but **no pixel dimensions**. So I can't state the current over-provisioning factor from the JSON alone — check the intrinsic size and the CSS render box before encoding. The numbers below assume a conventional full-bleed hero. **Target dimensions.** Size to the visible render area, then serve a responsive set rather than one file: | Variant | Width | Serves | |---|---|---| | `hero-640` | 640 px | phones @1x–2x | | `hero-960` | 960 px | small tablets | | `hero-1280` | 1280 px | laptops @1x | | `hero-1920` | 1920 px | desktop @1x / laptop @2x | Cap the master at **1920 px wide**. Beyond that you're paying real bytes for pixels no one resolves — a hero photo at 2× on a 1440 px container is past the point where more data reads as more sharpness. Match the aspect ratio to the CSS box (commonly 16:9 or ~3:1 for a banner strip) so you're not shipping pixels that `object-fit: cover` crops off. Wire it up with `srcset` + `sizes` so the browser picks; keep `width`/`height` attributes to reserve layout space and protect CLS. Realistic budget: **under 100 KB for the 1920 variant, ~25–40 KB at 640.** That's a 60–90% cut from 253.9 KB. **Format: AVIF primary, WebP fallback, in a ``.** ```html ``` Why AVIF as the primary for *this* asset specifically: - **Compression.** On photographic hero content AVIF typically lands 30–50% below WebP at matched perceptual quality. On a hero, that difference is the whole LCP argument. - **Gradients.** Heroes are the classic banding victim — big smooth skies, brand gradients, soft vignettes. WebP's 8-bit 4:2:0 chroma bands visibly there; AVIF supports 10/12-bit and holds gradients cleanly at low bitrates. This is the failure mode most likely to make a designer reject the re-encode, so it's the one to design around. - **Support is no longer the blocker** — Chrome, Firefox, Safari 16+, Edge. The `` fallback covers the tail for free. Why WebP still ships as the second `` rather than being skipped: universal support, and it's a trivial second encode. Don't make it the *only* format — that leaves the largest single win on the table. And **do not keep PNG in the chain**; PNG is lossless and the wrong tool for a photographic hero at any size. (If it turns out the "hero" is flat-color vector artwork rather than a photograph, that changes the answer entirely — see this scan's `suggested_action` on the finding, which flags exactly that: *"If the asset is decorative, consider whether an SVG icon or CSS gradient would replace it entirely."* An SVG or CSS gradient would take it to near-zero bytes.) **Concrete encode:** ```bash magick hero-banner.png -resize 1920x hero-1920.png avifenc --min 0 --max 63 -a end-usage=q -a cq-level=28 -s 4 hero-1920.png hero-1920.avif cwebp -q 78 -m 6 hero-1920.png -o hero-1920.webp ``` Tune `cq-level` (lower = higher quality; 24–32 is the usable hero band) and eyeball the gradient regions at full-bleed on a good display before committing. Repeat per width. ### One follow-up This PR is the third asset finding in the same repo — `hero-banner.png` (254 KB PNG), `partner-logo.svg` (two base64 rasters inside an SVG, severity `high`), `check-icon.png` (32×32 raster that should be an SVG). Individually each is `quick`/`small` effort. Together they say there's no image pipeline. Worth a separate issue to add build-time responsive encoding rather than fixing these one asset per PR.
